# Near-Optimal In-Place Sorting **Alex Z. Xu**1 \(\unknown\)
Independent Researcher, Hong Kong **Stephen J. Chick** \(\unknown\)
Independent Researcher, Commerce City, CO, USA **Abstract** We present an in-place comparison-based sorting algorithm that sorts an array of _n_ elements using _n_lg_n+O(n_) comparisons with exponentially high probability and always _O(n_) moves. This serves as the first in-place sorting algorithm to match the fundamental \(nlgn+\Omega(n)\) lower bound on total operations (i.e. sum of comparisons and moves). For the worst-case, we present an algorithm that makes _n_lg_n+O(n_lg(_t_)_n_) comparisons and _O(tn_) data moves, where _t_ is an integer parameter satisfying \(2\le t\le lg^*n-1\) and lg(_t_)_n_ denotes the _t_-time iterated logarithm, improving over the previous upper bound of _n_lg_n+O(n_lggl_n_) comparisons and _O(n_) moves when using constant _t\>_2. When _t_≈lg∗_n_, this yields a worst-case upper bound on total operations of _n_lg_n+O(n_lg∗_n_). We thus achieve the ultimate goal of efficient in-place sorting via randomization whilst narrowing the gap to this goal in the worst-case. This advance involves a novel ordered set structure that supports searches in an optimal lg_n+O_(1) comparisons for _n_ elements. Note that both algorithms are unstable. **2012 ACM Subject Classification** Theory of computation \(\rightarrow\) Sorting and searching **Keywords and phrases** sorting, in-place algorithms, data structures, computational complexity 1 Corresponding author

## 1 Introduction

Sorting is one of the most fundamental problems in computer science, carrying great practical and theoretical importance. For a comparison-based sort on a data set of _n_ elements, it is well known that the information-theoretic lower bound is lg(_n_!)≈_n_lg_n_-1.4427_n_ comparisons, which also holds for the average case, and at least ⌊1.5_n_⌋ moves are required to permute the input [11]. Summing gives a lower bound on total operations (i.e. sum of comparisons and moves) of ≈_n_lg_n_+0.0573_n_. Note that all logarithms throughout this paper are base 2.

In-place sorting is essential for large datasets in memory-constrained environments. A strict in-place algorithm uses only a single extra element storage location aside from the input array to permute elements and _O_(1) auxiliary words of size at least lg_n_ bits for tracking.

Simultaneously minimizing comparisons, moves, and auxiliary workspace represents a classic frontier in the complexity of sorting, dating back to foundational limits established by Munro and Raman, i.e. to achieve minimal comparisons under _O(n_) moves and in-place constraints. Currently, the tightest upper bound (for both average and worst-case behavior) is _n_lg_n+O(n_lggl_n_) comparisons and \((34+\varepsilon)n\) moves [4].

Whether the _O(n_glgl_n_) term could be reduced was left as an open problem. In this paper we resolve this open problem by presenting two variations of our in-place algorithm: a randomized and deterministic approach. Both variations are unstable. For any input, the randomized approach performs _n_lg_n+O(n_) comparisons with exponentially high probability (over the algorithm’s random choices) and always _O(n_) moves. This probabilistically achieves the ultimate goal of in-place sorting with minimal extra comparisons and moves (see [4, 10]), and matches the total operation lower bound of _n_lg_n_+0.0573_n_ up to an additive linear term. The deterministic approach makes _n_lg_n+O(n_lg<sup>(_t_)</sup>_n_) comparisons and _O(tn_) moves in the worst case, where _t_ is an integer parameter satisfying \(2\le t\le lg^*n-1\), thereby narrowing the gap to this ultimate goal: using constant _t\>_2 yields a definitive improvement over [4]. Total operations are minimized when _t_≈lg<sup>∗</sup>_n_: comparisons reach the optimal _n_lg_n+O(n_), whilst the move count degenerates slightly to _O(n_lg<sup>∗</sup>_n_).

### 1.1 Technical Overview

In Section 2, we detail the two-level structure reminiscent of y-fast tries in [12] that is used to facilitate sorting assuming the existence of additional memory:

The upper level is an ordered set containing _s<sub>#</sub> active representatives_ that supports searches in l_gs<sub>#</sub>+O_(1) comparisons and insertions in _O_(lg<sup>3</sup>_s<sub>#</sub>_) time (see Section 2.2).

Each active representative corresponds to lower-level _segment_, which is a block of size \(s=\Theta(lg^4s_#)\).

The upper level’s optimal search is used to route inserted elements towards segments. Elements are temporarily stored in a cache line (see Sections 2.4 and 2.6) within an active representative before they are flushed into segments in batches. Only when a segment becomes full and is split into two segments each containing half the elements, is a new active representative inserted for the new segment, ensuring costly upper level insertions are sparse.

Although the upper level maintains the sorted order of segments, elements in segments are kept unsorted until extraction, where they are sorted by the procedure in Section 2.3.

Lastly, in Section 3 we demonstrate a method to carve out the additional memory directly from the input array, thus achieving truly in-place sorting.

The key improvements over [4] are: the new ordered set, two optimized cache structures, and optimal segment sorting. Each change shaves off an independent _O(n_glgl_n_) term in comparisons, thus all three are required simultaneously to yield an improved bound.

## 2 Sorting with Additional Memory

Before considering the full in-place algorithm, we address a simpler problem. We are given:

A contiguous block _A_ of exactly _m_ elements, called _active elements_.

A contiguous _buffer memory B_ of at least 3_m_-1 _buffer elements_. Buffer elements can be distinguished from active elements using 1 comparison. Formally, there exists a function active(_x_) that makes 1 comparison then returns a Boolean `true` if _x_ is an active element and `false` otherwise (i.e. _x_ is a buffer element).

A bit vector _V_ containing at least _m/_lg<sup>2</sup>_m_ bits, all initialized to `false`. The bit vector supports exclusively single-bit operations: _V_.read(_i_) costing 1 comparison which returns a boolean value indicating the value of the _i_th bit and _V_.write(_i_) which flips the _i_th bit costing 3 moves.

_O_(1) auxiliary words of width \(\ge\mathrm{lg}m\) bits and a single empty location, i.e. the _hole_; from the original in-place sorting setting.

The objective is to sort the _m_ active elements in _A_, making use of _B_ and _V_ as additional workspaces. When the program terminates, _B_ must be some permutation of its original elements, and _V_ must be reset to its initial blank state. Note that _B_ and _V_ serve as temporary mathematical abstractions of in-place mechanisms that will be fully detailed below in Section 3. If required, see [App. E] for a complete notation glossary.

### 2.1 Structure of the Memory

In this section we detail the high-level layout of our provided additional workspaces.

**The buffer memory** _B_ consists of three main sections arranged sequentially: the _frame memory F_, _cache memory G_ and _segment memory S_, retaining the frame-cache-segments organization established in [4]. **The bit vector** _V_ contains the _pointer memory P_ and the _cache data I_ arranged sequentially.

**The segment memory** _S_ forms the lower level of the structure, serving as the primary storage of active elements. The segment memory consists of _s_<sub>#</sub>+1 segments _S_<sub>0</sub>_...S_<sub>_s_<sub>#</sub></sub>, each a contiguous block of

\(s=2\lceil\mathrm{lg}m\rceil^3g-1\) (1)

elements, where \(g=\Theta(\mathrm{lg}m)\) is defined later in (4), giving us \(s=\Theta(\mathrm{lg}^4m)\). Physically in _S_, the segments are not necessarily stored sequentially in the order _S_<sub>0</sub>_...S_<sub>_s_<sub>#</sub></sub>; they can be arranged in any permutation with _S_<sub>0</sub> at the front. The _segment invariant_ mandates that each segment contains between \(\lfloor s/2\rfloor\) and _s_ active elements placed contiguously at the front.

Segments are dynamically allocated from a reserved zone of 2_m_ elements in _B_, divided into \(\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\) blocks of _s_ elements \(B_0\dots B_{\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor-1}\) (any remaining elements at the end are excluded). Initially, there is only one segment _S_<sub>0</sub>. To allocate a new segment, we increment _s_<sub>#</sub> and return the next available block in the reserved zone (_B_<sub>_s_<sub>#</sub></sub>). Immediately after allocation, \(\lfloor s/2\rfloor\) active elements are moved into the new segment to fulfill the segment invariant.

Every segment _S<sub>i</sub>_ has a corresponding **active representative** \(R'_i\) in the upper level to coordinate routing into segments. These _s_<sub>#</sub> active representatives \(R'_1\dots R'_{s_\#}\) form a subset of _r_<sub>#</sub> pre-allocated _representatives_ denoted by _R_<sub>1</sub>_...R_<sub>_r_<sub>#</sub></sub>. Any remaining non-active representatives are classified as _buffer representatives_. Each representative _R<sub>i</sub>_ is a compound data type formed by _f<sub>i</sub>_, _P<sub>i</sub>_, _G<sub>i</sub>_ and _I<sub>i</sub>_ (defined shortly).

Specifically, the first component _f<sub>i</sub>_ is a _frame element_, and together _f_<sub>1</sub>_...f_<sub>_r_<sub>#</sub></sub> constitute the **frame memory** _F_. _F_ consists of _s_<sub>#</sub> active elements interleaved with buffer elements; _f<sub>i</sub>_ is active iff _R<sub>i</sub>_ is active. The _active frame elements_ form the sequence \(f'_1\dots f'_{s_\#}\) obtained

## 4 Near-Optimal In-Place Sorting

by scanning _f_<sub>1</sub>_...f_<sub>_r_#</sub> ignoring buffer elements. This sequence is maintained as a sorted sequence by the structure in Section 2.2. The active frame elements define the _ordering invariant_ that maintains relative sorted order across segments: for any active element \(x\in S_i\), \(f'_i\le x\le f'_{i+1}\) (logical sentinels \(f'_0=-\infty\), \(f'_{s_\#+1}=\infty\)).

By the segment invariant, there are at least \(\lfloor s/2\rfloor\) active elements in each of the _s_#+1 segments, and also _s_# active elements reside in the frame. Because the total number of active elements cannot exceed _m_, we conclude that _s_# is at most

\(s_\#\le\lfloor(m-\lfloor s/2\rfloor)/(\lfloor s/2\rfloor+1)\rfloor\le\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor-1\) (2)

Consequently, the size of segment memory is bounded by:

\(|S|=(s_\#+1)s\le 2m\) (3)

Thus, the segment memory cannot surpass the reserved zone of size 2_m_.

Due to the arbitrary arrangement of the segments in the segment memory, we cannot easily locate the segment _S<sub>i</sub>_ corresponding with \(R'_i\). Thus, we introduce the **pointer memory** _P_ in _V_ , consisting of the _segment pointers P_<sub>1</sub>_...P_<sub>_r_#</sub>. Let the _active segment pointers_ be \(P'_1\dots P'_{s_\#}\), corresponding with the active representatives \(R'_1\dots R'_{s_\#}\). Each _P<sub>i</sub>_ is a block of \(\lfloor lg\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\rfloor+1\) bits, sufficient to address any of the \(\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\) blocks in the reserved zone by encoding an integer in binary: if \(P'_i=k\), then _S<sub>i</sub>_ occupies the block _B<sub>k</sub>_. For all segment pointers corresponding with a buffer representative, _P<sub>i</sub>_=0 representing a NIL pointer as there is no corresponding segment.

However, dereferencing a segment pointer would require \(\lfloor lg\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\rfloor+1\) reads in _V_ using _O_(lg_m_) comparisons. To minimize overhead, we utilize one pointer dereference to operate upon a batch of _g_ elements, reducing the per-element cost of dereferencing pointers to _O_(lg_m)/g=O_(1) (see (4) below). Batch operations are facilitated by the **cache memory** _G_ using its _r_# _cache lines G_<sub>1</sub>_...G_<sub>_r_#</sub>, each a block of 2_g_ elements operating as a specialized structure used to accumulate _g_ active elements, where

\(lgm\le g\le 2lgm\) (4)

For now, assume that a cache line _G<sub>i</sub>_ is a black box that supports the operations _G<sub>i</sub>_.insert(_x_) and _G<sub>i</sub>_.flush(_x_). _G<sub>i</sub>_.insert(_x_) exchanges the active element at _x_ with a buffer element in _G<sub>i</sub>_, then returns a Boolean indicating whether _G<sub>i</sub>_ has become full. _G<sub>i</sub>_.flush(_x_) swaps the active elements in _G<sub>i</sub>_ with the contiguous block of buffer elements beginning at _x_. The cost of cache operations will be accounted for in _cache inserts_ (calls of insert) and _cache flushes_ (calls of flush). The exact implementation of cache lines is specified in Section 2.6.

Initially, all cache lines consist of only buffer elements. The _active cache line_ \(G'_i\) corresponding with \(R'_i\) temporarily stores active elements belonging in _S<sub>i</sub>_, waiting until it accumulates _g_ active elements so they are flushed into _S<sub>i</sub>_ as a batch. Thus, the ordering invariant that applies to _S<sub>i</sub>_ must also apply to \(G'_i\).

To support cache lines in their operations, the **cache data** _I_ in _V_ stores _r_# _cache integers I_<sub>1</sub>_...I_<sub>_r_#</sub>, each a block of \(\lfloor lgg\rfloor+1\) bits, used to store integers from 0 to _g_. Each cache line _G<sub>i</sub>_ may use its corresponding cache integer _I<sub>i</sub>_ to assist its operations.

To maintain a 1:1 correspondence between active representatives and segments, after a new segment is allocated, a corresponding active representative is constructed from a buffer representative _R<sub>i</sub>_ and an active element _x_ promoted to the frame. This requires _O_(lg_m_) moves: swap _x_ with _f<sub>i</sub>_ (which makes _R<sub>i</sub>_ active), then assign _P<sub>i</sub>_:=_s_# so it points to the _s_#th block in the reserved zone, i.e. the newly allocated segment.

Testing whether a representative _R<sub>i</sub>_ is active requires a single comparison by active(_f<sub>i</sub>_). The rank of _R<sub>i</sub>_ is defined by its frame element, meaning _R<sub>i</sub>\<R<sub>j</sub>_ iff _f<sub>i</sub>\<f<sub>j</sub>_. To compare an active element _x_ and _R<sub>i</sub>_, compare _x_ and _f<sub>i</sub>_ directly. Exchanging two representatives _R<sub>i</sub>_ and _R<sub>j</sub>_ is done by exchanging each component individually: _f<sub>i</sub>_ with _f<sub>j</sub>_, _G<sub>i</sub>_ with _G<sub>j</sub>_, _P<sub>i</sub>_ with _P<sub>j</sub>_, and _I<sub>i</sub>_ with _I<sub>j</sub>_; the process requires _O_(lg_m_) comparisons and _O_(lg_m_) moves.

_S_<sub>0</sub> is unique in the sense that it has no corresponding active representative and is handled separately by the auxiliary pointers _l_<sub>0</sub> to the next buffer position in _S_<sub>0</sub> and _r_<sub>0</sub> to the end of _S_<sub>0</sub>.

## 2.2 Structure of Representatives

Let _R_ denote the collection of all _r_<sub>#</sub> representatives. We structure _R_ to support the operations _R._search(_x_) and _R._insert(_x_) efficiently. _R._search(_x_) finds the active representative \(R'_i\) such that \(f'_i\le x\le f'_{i+1}\), and returns its position in _R_, or 0 if \(x<f'_1\). _R._insert(_x_) adds a new active representative into _R_ for a newly allocated segment with _x_ as its active frame element. Full procedural descriptions and formal analysis of the operations are available in [App. A].

_R_ consists of the _library L_ at the front and the _rebuild buffer D_ at the back.

**The library** _L_ contains the sorted sequence of all active representatives interlaced with buffer representatives, which serve as slack space for efficient insertions. _L_ behaves like a dynamic array, beginning at the left of a reserved zone of \(8\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\) buffer representatives and expands rightwards.

At any moment, the number of active representatives is _s_<sub>#</sub> as there are exactly _s_<sub>#</sub> active frame elements. Let \(s'_\#=2\lfloor lgs_\#\rfloor\le s_\#\) denote the number of active representatives at the previous resize. _L_ consists of \(s'_\#\) _gaps L_<sub>1</sub>_...L_<sub>_s_<sub>#</sub></sub>, each a block of 8 representatives \(\ell_1\dots\ell_8\). Using (2) to bound |_L_|

\(|L|\le 8s'_\#\le 8s_\#\le 8\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\)

Each **gap** _L<sub>i</sub>_ has the form _a_<sub>1</sub>_...a<sub>k</sub>b_<sub>_k_+1</sub>_...b_<sub>8</sub>, where _a<sub>i</sub>_ are active representatives in sorted order and _b<sub>i</sub>_ are buffer representatives. The _gap invariant_ requires 0_\<k\<_8, so each gap contains at least one active and one buffer representative. The sequence \(L'_1\dots L'_{s_\#}\) where \(L'_i\) denotes the active representatives in _L<sub>i</sub>_ forms the global sorted sequence of all active representatives. At startup, _s_<sub>#</sub>=0, but we pre-allocate one gap _L_<sub>1</sub> containing only buffer representatives and set \(s'_\#=1\).

## 6 Near-Optimal In-Place Sorting

**The rebuild buffer** _D_ is a contiguous block of fixed size \(\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\) representatives. Typically, _D_ consists only of buffer representatives, but active representatives are temporarily stored in _D_ during rebalancing. By (2), |_D|\>s_<sub>#</sub>, so _D_ can hold every active representative.

This gives the total number of representatives

\(r_\#=|L|+|D|\le 8\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor+\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor=9\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\) (5)

It follows that the required size of the frame memory, cache memory, and bit vector are respectively

\(|F|=r_\#\le 9\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\le 9m/lg^4m,\) (6)

\(|G|=r_\#2g\approx 18m/lg^3m,\) (7)

\(|V|=r_\#\left(\lfloor lg\lfloor 2m/s\rfloor\rfloor+\lfloor lgg\rfloor+2\right)\approx 9m/lg^3m\le m/lg^2m,\) (8)

for sufficiently large _m_. From (3), (6), (7), the required size of the buffer memory is then

\(|B|=|F|+|G|+|S|\le 3m-1\) (9)

**The operation** _R._search(_x_) is implemented by two binary searches to locate the final active representative \(R_y\le x\). The outer search locates the last gap _L<sub>i</sub>_ among \(L_1\dots L_{s_\#^\prime}\) whose first representative \(\ell_1\le x\), leveraging the existence of an active representative at the front of every gap by the gap invariant to guarantee a contiguous, monotonic search space. The second binary search then locates the exact last representative \(\ell_j\le x\) within the isolated gap, returning its position. Because \(R'_z=R_y\) is the last active representative \(\le x\), the next active representative \(R'_{z+1}>x\). Thus, it obeys the ordering invariant \(f'_z\le x<f'_{z+1}\).

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 2.1.** _R.search(x_) _requires_ \(lgs'_\#+3=\lfloor lgs_\#\rfloor+3\) _comparisons._

**Proof.** The outer binary search costs \(lgs'_\#\) comparisons exactly since \(s'_\#\) is a power of 2. The inner search then requires lg8=3 comparisons. Summing gives \(\lfloor lgs_\#\rfloor+3\) comparisons. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

**The operation** _R._insert(_x_) is implemented by first locating the position where _x_ belongs by _R._search(_x_). Then, by a standard array-based linear shift within the gap implemented with exchanges, we shift a buffer representative from the back of the gap _x_ belongs in to the desired location, making room for _x_ to be constructed in its sorted position, maintaining the sorted order of active frame elements. To ensure that a buffer representative is always present at the end of the gap for future insertions, we verify if the gap invariant still holds, executing dynamic rebalancing to restore the invariant if it was violated by the insertion. Occasionally when \(s_\#=2s'_\#\) a resize exchanges all active representatives into _D_ and rebuilds the library structure with _s_<sub>#</sub> gaps each containing one active representative, updating \(s'_\#:=s_\#=2s'_\#\).

**Dynamic rebalancing** uses an imaginary segment tree over the gaps \(L_1\dots L_{s_\#^\prime}\) with nodes \(n_1\dots n_{2s_\#^\prime-1}\), where _n_<sub>1</sub> is the root node _covering_ all gaps, and leaves \(n_{s_\#^\prime}\dots n_{2s_\#^\prime-1}\) correspond with individual gaps. The nodes are indexed like a binary tree. For each node _n<sub>k</sub>_ covering the range _L<sub>l</sub>...L<sub>r</sub>_, let size(_n<sub>k</sub>_) denote the number of active representatives in the range, and let span(_n<sub>k</sub>_)=_r-l_+1, i.e. the size of the range. The rebalancing strategy is inspired by lazy weight balancing in scapegoat trees from [3]. When we encounter a full gap _L<sub>i</sub>_, we traverse towards the root from its corresponding leaf node _n<sub>j</sub>_ where \(j=i+s'_\#-1\) (with size(_n<sub>j</sub>_)=8). At every step of the traversal, a linear scan counts \(size\left(n_{j\oplus 1}\right)\) (i.e. the sibling’s size), then we compute \(size\left(n_{\lfloor j/2\rfloor}\right)=size\left(n_j\right)+size\left(n_{j\oplus 1}\right)\), and set \(j:=\lfloor j/2\rfloor\), moving to the parent. This process repeats until we encounter a _scapegoat node n<sub>j</sub>_ that satisfies

\(|size\left(n_{2j}\right)-size\left(n_{2j+1}\right)|>max\left(1,size\left(n_j\right)/lgs'_\#\right)\) (10)

Because the size of the children of a node _n<sub>j</sub>_ that does not satisfy (10) are bounded by \(\lfloor\mathrm{size}(n_j)/2\rfloor+\mathrm{max}(1,\mathrm{size}(n_j)/\mathrm{lg}s'_\#)\), repeating this linear recurrence down from the root to a leaf bounds the leaf size by 2_e_+1 (where _e_≈2.71 is Euler’s constant). But as _L<sub>i</sub>_ is full containing 8_\>_2_e_+1 active representatives, we know a scapegoat node that satisfies (10) must exist on the path.

The subtree rooted at the scapegoat node is then rebuilt: move all _z_ active representatives into _D_, then redistribute them evenly across the gaps in the subtree so that for every internal node _n<sub>k</sub>_ in the subtree \(0\le\mathrm{size}(n_{2k})-\mathrm{size}(n_{2k+1})\le 1\). To compute the block of active representatives for each gap, we conduct an in-order traversal of the subtree with a stack of one bit per tree level packed into _O_(1) words that allows us to recalculate the correct block for each ancestor node [App. A]. Upon reaching a leaf node, we transport the correct block into the gap. Because the sizes of the scapegoat node’s children differ by at least 2 by condition (10), at least one child is forced to fall strictly below its maximum capacity. This limits \(\mathrm{size}(n_j)\le 7\mathrm{span}(n_j)\), ensuring that an even redistribution leaves at most 7 active representatives per gap, restoring the gap invariant. The process rearranges the positions of active representatives, invalidating the location returned by previous _R_.search operations.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 2.2.** _R.insert(x_) _requires O_(lg<sup>3</sup>_m) comparisons and O_(lg<sup>3</sup>_m) moves amortized._

**Proof.** Excluding the cost of rebalancing, insertions cost _O_(lg_m_) amortized: the initial search is _O_(lg_m_), the linear shift conducts _O_(1) representative exchanges as the size of gaps is constant, and the \(2s'_\#\) representative exchanges conducted by resizing are spread among the \(s'_\#/2\) insertions since the previous resize to _O_(1) representative exchanges per insertion.

To bound rebalancing costs, we use the accounting method. For each internal node _n<sub>k</sub>_, let \(\psi\left(n_k\right)=\mathrm{max}\left(0,\left|\mathrm{size}\left(n_{2k}\right)-\mathrm{size}\left(n_{2k+1}\right)\right|-1\right)\) denote its _imbalance_. Now consider an instance of rebalancing that rebuilds a subtree of size _z_. The traversal to find a scapegoat node costs _z_=size(_n<sub>j</sub>_) comparisons, as 1 comparison is used to count each active representative [App. A]. The rebuild then swaps each representative into then out of _z_ using 2_z_ representative exchanges costing _O(z_lg_m_), resetting imbalance in the subtree to 0. By condition (10), prior to the rebuild the subtree contained \(\Omega(z/\mathrm{lg}s'_\#)\) units of imbalance, so each unit of imbalance is repaired at \(O(z\mathrm{lg}m)/\Omega(z/\mathrm{lg}s'_\#)=O(\mathrm{lg}^2m)\) cost. Inserting a new active representative increases the size of a leaf node by 1, which may increase the imbalance of each of its \(\mathrm{lg}s'_\#\) ancestors by 1. Each unit incurred may later be repaired at _O_(lg<sup>2</sup>_m_) cost, bounding the cost of dynamic rebalancing at _O_(lg<sup>3</sup>_m_) amortized. Combining costs gives the overall bound. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

## 2.3 Sorting Small Subsequences

We now introduce a specialized _small sort_ that is designed to sort small subsequences \(A'\) of \(m'=O(\mathrm{lg}^cm)\) active elements for some constant _c_ given a _merge buffer_ \(B'\) of \(m'\) buffer elements, the hole, and _O_(1) auxiliary words of \(w\ge\mathrm{lgm}\) bits, adapted from [8]. This subroutine is used during extraction to sort segments. The algorithm is implemented as a _k_-way merge sort, where

\(k=2^{\lceil\mathrm{lg}(w/\mathrm{lg}\mathrm{lg}m)\rceil}\ge\mathrm{lgm}/\mathrm{lglgm}\)

It begins by sorting runs of size _k_ by table sort from [9] with merge sort on the pointers. Subsequently, adjacent groups of _k_ runs are merged by using a selection tree to repeatedly select the minimum element from the current front of all runs. The choice of _k_ as a power of 2 ensures the selection tree forms a perfect binary tree, minimizing overhead. The pointer array and selection tree occupy \(O(k)\left(\lfloor\mathrm{lg}m'\rfloor+1\right)=O(w)\) bits, which is packed into _O_(1)

words. This process repeats until the entire block \(A'\) is a contiguous sorted run. This requires \(k_\#=\lceil lgm'/lgk\rceil-1\) passes of merging. The use of table sort in the first phase is to avoid the overhead of constructing the selection tree in the second merging phase. For the formal step-by-step procedure and extended analysis, see [App. B].

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 2.3.** _For any constant c, a sequence of_ \(m'=O(lg^cm)\) _active elements can be sorted using no more than_ \(m'lgm'+o(m')\) _comparisons and_ \(O(m')\) _movies if given a merge buffer of_ \(m'\) _buffer elements._

**Proof.** Each merge pass requires at most \(m'lgk+O(m')\) comparisons. In the final pass, there are only \(k'=\left\lceil m'/k^{k_\#}\right\rceil\) runs, so it needs only \(m'\left\lceil lgk'\right\rceil+O(m')\) comparisons. Summing over the initial run sorting and all merge passes, the total comparison cost satisfies

**i.** Select the median element _a_med of _S<sub>z</sub>_ by the linear-time stable, in-place selection algorithm of [6] then stably ternary partition _S<sub>z</sub>_ around pivot _a_med [7], logically dividing the block =_a_med at the midpoint of _S<sub>z</sub>_. This leaves the elements of _S<sub>z</sub>_ in the configuration \(a_1\dots a_{\lfloor s/2\rfloor} a_\text{med}a'_1\dots a'_{\lfloor s/2\rfloor}\) where \(a_i\le a_\text{med}\le a'_i\) for all \(1\le i\le\lfloor s/2\rfloor\).

**ii.** Allocate the new segment _S_<sub>_z_+1</sub>, which returns a pointer to its start.

## 2.5 Extracting in Sorted Order

The extraction phase transports all active elements back to _A_ in sorted order. After insertion completes, every active element lies either in the frame, cache or segments, whilst _A_ contains only buffer elements.

By a linear scan through the _L_, for every active representative \(R'_i\), \(G'_i\) is emptied into _Si_ by the same method as step 3 of insertion. In total, _o(m_) comparisons and _s_# cache flushes are required to empty all cache lines. This leaves active elements either as active frame elements \(f'_1\dots f'_{s_\#}\) in sorted order or in segments _S_<sub>0</sub>_...S<sub>s<sub>#</sub></sub>_, where for any \(a_i\in S_i\), the ordering invariant \(f'_i\le a_i\le f'_{i+1}\) holds. It follows that, the sequence \(S'_0f'_1S'_1f'_2\dots f'_{s_\#}S'_{s_\#}\) is the sorted sequence of all _m_ active elements, where \(S'_i\) denotes the sorted sequence of all active elements in _Si_. We now construct this sequence in _A_.

First, we transport \(S'_0\) to the front of _A_. We sort the active elements in _S_<sub>0</sub> (from _l_<sub>0</sub> to _r_<sub>0</sub>) with the small sort using _A_ as the merge buffer, then move the sorted block to the front of _A_.

Next, we linearly scan through _L_ from left to right. for each active representative \(R'_i\) we encounter, we conduct the following:

**1.** Swap the element \(f'_i\) with the next available buffer space in _A_.

**2.** Read the corresponding active segment pointer \(p:=P'_i\) to locate the physical position of _Si_.

**3.** Perform a binary search over _Si_ to find the number of active elements in _Si_, denoted by _si_. Let the active elements in _Si_ be _a_<sub>1</sub>_...a<sub>si</sub>_.

**4.** Using _S_<sub>0</sub> (already emptied) as the merge buffer, sort _a_<sub>1</sub>_...a<sub>si</sub>_ with the small sort.

**5.** Move _a_<sub>1</sub>_...a<sub>si</sub>_ into the next _si_ buffer positions in _A_.

Every iteration adds the sequence of active elements \(f'_iS'_i\) to the end of the growing sorted sequence in _A_. Since active representatives appear in sorted order in _L_, the resulting sequence in _A_ is exactly \(S'_0f'_1S'_1f'_2\dots f'_{s_\#}S'_{s_\#}\), the global sorted sequence of all _m_ active elements.

Finally, to fulfill the Section 2 termination requirements, we verify the ending states of _B_ and _V_ . Throughout, the algorithm writes elements only by swapping (via hole :=_a_, _a_:=_b_, _b_:= hole), which exclusively permutes elements. Since the final sorted permutation of all active elements is in _A_, then the remaining elements in _B_ are already a permutation of the original buffer elements. However, the bit vector remains modified, requiring a linear scan to reset it to all `false`, using |_V_|=_o(m_) comparisons and at most 3|_V_|=_o(m_) moves (see (8)). Subsequently the algorithm terminates safely.

## 2.6 Structure of Cache Lines

We now specify the two different designs for cache lines (defined in Section 2.1).

First, consider the _randomized cache line_ used in the **randomized approach**. We choose _g_=2<sup>⌊lglg_m_⌉</sup>, which satisfies (4). Let us denote: the cache line as the block of elements _g_<sub>1</sub>_...g_<sub>2_g_</sub>, and the corresponding cache integer as _d_, with bits _d_<sub>0</sub>_...d_lg_g_, where bit _d<sub>i</sub>_ has weight 2_<sup>i</sup>_. This is well defined as _g_ is a power of 2.

The process of insert(_x_) in a randomized cache line works as follows:

**1.** Probe for a buffer slot. Repeatedly select a uniformly random index \(j\in[1\dots 2g]\), check whether _g<sub>j</sub>_ is a buffer element, and retry if it is active until a buffer position _g<sub>j</sub>_ is found.

**2.** Swap the active element _x_ with _g<sub>j</sub>_, placing _x_ in the cache line.

**3.** Increment _d_ to reflect the new active element.

**4.** Return the state of the cache line (full or not), given by the value of the bit _d_lg_g_ with priority _g_.

Randomized cache lines store data sparsely like hash tables for constant-time insertions: at most _g_ active elements are spread among 2_g_ slots, capping the load factor at 1/2, so the expected number of probes is 1/(1-1/2)=2, each requiring one comparison. Then, the swap requires 3 moves. The increment of _d_ is _O_(1) amortized by aggregate analysis. Finally, checking for fullness requires reading the bit _d_lg_g_ using one comparison. In total, each insertion requires _O_(1) comparisons expected and _O_(1) moves amortized (see [App. C] for a more comprehensive analysis).

The operation _G<sub>i</sub>_.flush(_x_) is a simple linear scan with swaps. Iterating through _g_<sub>1</sub>_...g_<sub>2_g_</sub>, identify every active element _g<sub>j</sub>_, and swap _g<sub>j</sub>_ with the next available buffer space after _x_. Lastly, reset the cache integer by _d_:=0. This process uses 2_g_ comparisons and \(\le 3g+3\) moves.

**Theorem 2.6.** _A sequence A of m active elements can be sorted using m_lg_m+O(m_) _comparisons with exponentially high probability and always O(m_) _moves if given a buffer memory B containing_ 3_m_-1 _buffer elements and bit vector V of size m/_lg<sup>2</sup>_m._

**Proof.** By instating the randomized cache line design, cache insertions cost _O_(1) comparisons expected and _O_(1) moves amortized and cache flushes cost _O(g_) comparisons and _O(g_) moves (shown directly above). Substituting these costs into Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5 then summing them gives _m_lg_m+O(m_) comparisons expected and _O(m_) moves deterministically. Over _m_ cache insertions, the probability of large deviations (i.e. _\>m_ comparisons above the expected amount) is bounded by (27/32)_<sup>m</sup>_ (see the Chernoff tail bound in [App. C]). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Next, we detail the mechanics of _deterministic cache lines_ for the **deterministic approach**. Deterministic cache lines consist of \(t'\) _cache blocks_ \(G_{t^\prime+1}\dots G_1\) from left to right, where _g<sub>i</sub>_=|_G<sub>i</sub>_| (we locally redefine _G<sub>i</sub>_ and _g<sub>i</sub>_ here). The block _G<sub>i</sub>_ consists of _g<sub>i</sub>/g_<sub>_i_-1</sub> _sub cache blocks A_<sub>1</sub>_...A<sub>j</sub>B_<sub>_j_+1</sub>_...B_<sub>_g<sub>i</sub>/g_<sub>_i_-1</sub> each of size _g_<sub>_i_-1</sub>, where _A_<sub>1</sub>_...A<sub>j</sub>_ contain only active elements and _B_<sub>_j_+1</sub>_...B_<sub>_g<sub>i</sub>/g_<sub>_i_-1</sub> contain only buffer elements.

The sizes are controlled by a parameter _t_ that satisfies \(2\le\left\lceil lg^{(t)}m\right\rceil\le lggm+1\). They are defined as _g_<sub>0</sub>=1, \(g_1=2^{\left\lceil lg^{(t)}m\right\rceil}\), and _g<sub>i</sub>=g_<sub>_i_-1</sub>2<sup>_g_<sub>_i_-1</sub>/2<sup>_i_-1</sup></sup> for all \(2\le i\le t'\), where \(t'\) is

the largest integer such that \(g_{t^\prime}<\mathrm{lg}m\). To account for any remaining space, we define the final term (overrides _g_<sub>1</sub> base case when \(t'=0\)):

\(g=g_{t^\prime+1}=g_{t^\prime}\lceil\mathrm{lg}m/g_{t^\prime}\rceil\le g_{t^\prime} 2^{g_{t^\prime}/2^{t^\prime-1}}\)

This ensures \(\mathrm{lg}m\le g\le 2\mathrm{lg}m\) as in (4), and that cache lines take up no more than 2_g_ spaces [App. C]. The recurrence makes _g<sub>i</sub>_ grow as a tower of exponentials, so the number of levels is proportional to _t_. It can be shown \(t'\le t-1\) by induction [App. C]. This growth also guarantees that the amortized comparison cost at levels \(i\ge 2\) form a convergent geometric series, shown shortly.

The procedure for insert(_x_) iterates through levels \(i=1\dots t'+1\). At every level:

**1.** Binary search in _G<sub>i</sub>_ for the next available sub cache block _B_<sub>_j_+1</sub> of buffer elements.

**2.** Swap the entire contents of the lower leveled cache block _G_<sub>_i_-1</sub> (or simply _x_ when _i_=1) into the found buffer block.

**3.** If this fills _G<sub>i</sub>_ (i.e. the last buffer block _B_<sub>_g<sub>i</sub>/g_<sub>_i_-1</sub> was used), we continue to level _i_+1, otherwise insertion completes returning 0.

If the loop ends without insert terminating, the last block \(G_{t^\prime+1}\) has been filled, and the cache line is full thus the procedure returns 1.

At level _i_, the lg(_g<sub>i</sub>/g_<sub>_i_-1</sub>) comparisons to locate a buffer block by binary search is spread among _g_<sub>_i_-1</sub> elements to lg(_g<sub>i</sub>/g_<sub>_i_-1</sub>)/_g_<sub>_i_-1</sub> comparisons per element. For \(i\ge 2\), the recurrence yields \(\mathrm{lg}\left(g_i/g_{i-1}\right)/g_{i-1}\le 1/2^{i-1}\). Summing over all levels, the total comparisons per element are \(\mathrm{lg}g_1+\sum_{i=2}^{t^\prime+1}1/2^{i-1}<\mathrm{lg}^{(t)}m+2\). Each element passes through every level once by a single swap costing 3 moves, which over all levels is \(3\left(t'+1\right)\le 3t\) moves.

The operation _G<sub>i</sub>_.flush(_x_) iterates through all cache blocks \(G_{t^\prime+1}\dots G_1\) in descending order of level, where for each cache block a binary search locates last sub cache block containing active elements _A<sub>j</sub>_, swapping all active elements in the cache block in _A_<sub>1</sub>_...A<sub>j</sub>_ to the next available buffer spaces after _x_. Because each level has _O_(lg_m_) sub cache blocks, each binary search costs _O_(lglg_m_) comparisons. With \(t'=O(\mathrm{lg}^*m)\) levels, the total comparisons are \(O(\mathrm{lg}\mathrm{lg}m\cdot\mathrm{lg}^*m)\). Each active element is swapped exactly once, totaling 3_g_ moves.

\(\blacktriangleright\) Remark 2.8. The deterministic additional memory algorithm is stable on the active elements, i.e. the relative order of equal active elements in the output is identical to the input. This does not apply to the randomized variant as active elements are placed arbitrarily in randomized cache lines. However, any in-place adaptation is unstable as the buffer memory is simulated by elements in the array, which are scrambled arbitrarily. If the buffer memory does not contain any equal array elements (e.g. if it is external or an explicitly collected distinct buffer), global stability holds. A full proof of this claim is in [App. C].

## 3 Sorting In-Place

Finally, we demonstrate how the buffer memory and bit vector used in Section 2 are carved out directly from the input array, following the in-place conversion technique of [2].

**The bit vector** is first created by using heapselect to isolate the smallest and largest \(v=\lceil n/lg^2n\rceil\) elements into the blocks _L=l_<sub>1</sub>_...l<sub>v</sub>_ and _R=r_<sub>1</sub>_...r<sub>v</sub>_ respectively, resulting in the configuration \(L\mathcal{A}'R\). Because _L_ and _R_ contain the smallest and largest elements in A, sorting \(\mathcal{A}'\) would sort A. This process requires _O(n+v_lg_n_)=_O(n_) time. The _i_th bit is encoded by the pair (_l<sub>i</sub>,r<sub>i</sub>_): if _l<sub>i</sub>\<r<sub>i</sub>_ the bit is 0, otherwise it is 1. The operation write(_i_) simply swaps _l<sub>i</sub>_ and _r<sub>i</sub>_. For this encoding to be valid, no pair can be equal, thus we test _l<sub>v</sub>\<r_<sub>1</sub>: if this is true the encoding is valid, otherwise the region \(\mathcal{A}'\) contains only one unique key and A is already sorted, allowing the algorithm to terminate immediately. As \(n\ge m\), \(\lceil n/lg^2n\rceil\ge m/lg^2m\), thus the bit vector is large enough to sort any subsequence of A using the algorithm from Section 2.

**The buffer memory** is then repeatedly created by a partition based loop. At the _i_th iteration, let \(\mathcal{A}'\) be subdivided into two regions _A<sub>S</sub>A<sub>U</sub>_, where all elements in _A<sub>S</sub>_ are in their correct sorted positions, and sorting _A<sub>U</sub>_ would sort \(\mathcal{A}'\). Initially _A<sub>S</sub>_ is empty. At the _i_th iteration, let the size of _A<sub>U</sub>_ be _n<sub>i</sub>_. Using the linear time in-place selection algorithm from [5], we select a pivot _p_ with rank \(\lceil n_i/4\rceil\) and partition _A<sub>U</sub>_ by _p_, resulting in the regions \(A_<pB_\ge\) where _A<sub><o></o></sub>_ contains _n<sub>i,<o></o></sub>_ elements _\<p_ and \(B_\ge\) contains elements \(\ge p\). Then, using \(B_\ge\) as the buffer memory and simulating _V_ with the blocks _L_ and _R_, we sort _A<sub><o></o></sub>_ by the additional memory algorithm from Section 2. Due to the classification of active and buffer elements relative to _p_, distinguishing active from buffer elements can be done by comparing against _p_: active(_x_) simply needs to return the Boolean result of _x\<p_. Because \(|A_<|\le\lceil n_i/4\rceil-1\) and \(|B_\ge|\ge n_i-\lceil n_i/4\rceil\), \(|B_\ge|\ge 3|A_<|-1\), the buffer size is sufficient. Lastly, we isolate all elements =_p_ in \(B_\ge\), resulting in the two blocks _P_ containing elements =_p_ and _B<sub>\></sub>_ holding the remaining elements. In the resulting sequence, the blocks _A<sub><o></o></sub>P_ are already in their correct sorted positions, thus we begin the next iteration with _B<sub>\></sub>=A<sub>U</sub>_. In each iteration, the selection and partitioning steps require _O(n<sub>i</sub>_) comparisons and _O(n<sub>i</sub>_) moves. Eventually, when |_A<sub>U</sub>|\<_2<sup>19</sup>=524288, the entire block _A<sub>U</sub>_ is sorted by table sort from Section 2.7 as a base case, and the algorithm terminates as A is sorted.

## 4 Concluding Remarks

In this paper, we have addressed the exact operational complexity of in-place sorting, establishing that the fundamental lower bound of \(nlgn+\Omega(n)\) total operations is tight for in-place randomized algorithms (with exponentially high probability). By resolving the previous inefficiencies present in [4] via introducing a novel ordered set, optimized cache structures, and an optimal small sort, we have achieved the ultimate goal stated in [4, 10] with exponentially high probability: sorting in-place using only _n_lg_n+O(n_) comparisons and _O(n_) moves.

We leave as an open problem the task of retaining the bound of _n_lg_n+O(n_) total operations in the worst case. The deterministic cache line stands as the only remaining obstacle to optimality, limiting the deterministic approach at _n_lg_n+O(n_lg<sup>(_t_)</sup>_n_) comparisons and _O(tn_) moves (where _t_ is an integer parameter satisfying \(2\le t\le lg*n-1\)), which results in a slightly looser total operation bound of _n_lg_n+O(n_lg<sup>∗</sup>_n_) when _t_≈lg<sup>∗</sup>_n_. However, this is sufficient to answer the open problem from [4] for improvements on their upper bound of _n_lg_n+O(n_lg_n_) comparisons and _O(n_) moves.

All in-place algorithms are unstable as the buffer elements are permuted arbitrarily. Whilst the deterministic additional memory algorithm is stable on active elements, it requires a completely distinct buffer to operate stably and in-place. As existing methods of collecting such a distinct buffer incur \(\Omega(nlgn)\) comparisons of overhead [1], we have not yet achieved a stable, in-place sorting algorithm that makes _n_lg_n+o(n_lg_n_) comparisons and _O(n_) moves (i.e. _n_lg_n+o(n_lg_n_) total operations). That problem remains open. The best known stable bound stands at _O(n_lg_n_) comparisons and _O(n_) moves [1].

## A Detailed Procedures and Proofs for Representatives Structure

Recall that there are _r<sub>#</sub>_ segment representatives out of which _s<sub>#</sub>_ are active, distributed among \(s'_\#\) gaps \(L_1\dots L_{s^\prime_\#}\), each a contiguous block of 8 representatives. Additionally, we also have the rebuild buffer _D_ that is large enough to hold all active representatives. Our objective is to support _R_.search(_x_) and _R_.insert(_x_) efficiently.

### A.1 Search

The operation _R_.search(_x_) finds the active representative \(R'_z\) such that \(f'_z\le x<f'_{z+1}\), and is implemented as two binary searches:

**1.** By an outer binary search in \(L_1\dots L_{s^\prime_\#}\), locate the last gap _Li_ whose first active representative \(\ell_1\) satisfies \(\ell_1\le x\).

**2.** By an inner binary search over \(Li_i=\ell_1\dots\ell_8\), find the first representative _l<sub>j</sub>_ that is either an active representative _\>x_ or a buffer representative (if no such active representative exists). The gap invariant guarantees such a segment representative exists (as a buffer representative must exist in the gap).

**3.** If _i_=1 and _j_=1, then _x\<f_<sub>1</sub>, thus _x_ belongs in _S_<sub>0</sub>; return 0. Otherwise, the correct active representative is \(\ell_{j-1}\), or _R<sub>y</sub>_ where _y_=8(_i_-1)+(_j_-1) in the global sequence _R_; return _y_.

Let the resulting active representative from _R_.search(_x_) be \(R'_z\). We show that \(f'_z\le x<f'_{z+1}\). By the outer binary search, _x_ lies between the first active representatives of _Li_ and _Li_+1. By the inner binary search, \(\ell_j\) is either the first active representative _\>x_ or the first buffer representative in _Li_. Therefore, \(\ell_{j-1}\) is the last active representative \(\le x\). The next active representative is either \(\ell_j\) which is _\>x_ by the inner binary search or the first representative of _Li_+1 which is also _\>x_ by the outer binary search. Thus, the inequality \(f'_z\le x<f'_{z+1}\) holds.

The outer binary search requires \(lgs'_\#\) comparisons exactly as \(s'_\#\) is a power of 2. The inner binary search requires exactly lg8=3 iterations as 8 is a power of 2. Naively, for each iteration, 2 comparisons are required to first determine if \(\ell_j\) is a buffer representative, then optionally an additional comparison against _x_ for active representatives. However, as buffer elements are greater than all active elements (see Section 3), a single comparison \(\ell_j>x\) suffices. Lastly, the edge case check and position calculation requires _O_(1) arithmetic operations.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma A.1.** _R.search(x_) _requires_ \(lgs'_\#+3=\lfloor lgs_\#\rfloor+3\) _comparisons._

### A.2 Insertion

The procedure for _R_.insert(_x_) is as follows:

**1.** Run _y=R_.search(_x_) to find the representative \(\ell_j\) from _Li_ (\(i=\lceil y/8\rceil\), _j=y_-8(_i_-1)), then increment _j_ giving position where _x_ should be inserted.

**2.** By a binary search in _Li_ find the last active representative _a<sub>k</sub>_ to determine the value of _k_, i.e. the number of active representatives in _Li_.

**3.** Iterating through \(j'=k\dots j\) (descending order), we swap every \(\ell_{j^\prime}\) with \(\ell_{j^\prime+1}\). This shifts the active representatives initially at \(\ell_j\dots\ell_k\) one unit rightwards into the positions \(\ell_{j+1}\dots\ell_{k+1}\), and \(\ell_j\) now contains the representative initially at \(\ell_{k+1}\), which is a buffer representative (as \(\ell_k\) is defined as the last active representative).

**4.** Construct the new active representative in \(\ell_j\), promoting _x_ to the frame.

**5.** Check if the gap invariant was violated, by verifying if _k_=7, as the insertion would add an additional active representative, creating a gap with 8 active representatives, violating the invariant. If so, execute the dynamic rebalancing procedure on _Li<sub>i</sub>_, which redistributes active representatives among other gaps to ensure the gap invariant is restored.

**6.** Verify if \(s_\#=2s'_\#\). If this is the case, the structure has reached its maximum capacity, and requires a resize operation that expands the library so it can hold more active representatives. The resulting library structure _L_ is made up of twice the gaps \(L_1\dots L_{s_\#}^{^\prime}\) where each gap _Li<sub>i</sub>_ contains a single active representative \(R'_i\) and 7 buffer representatives. The process is as follows:

**i.** Linearly scan through \(L_1\dots L_{s_\#}^{^\prime}\) for the active representatives \(R'_1\dots R'_{s_\#}\), exchanging them to a contiguous block at the front of _D_. The scanning process begins at the \(\ell_2\) of each gap as \(\ell_1\) is guaranteed to be active by the gap invariant and linearly scans rightwards until it meets a buffer representative, exchanging the found active representatives in the process.

**ii.** Transport all active representatives back into _L_, where \(R'_i\) is exchanged with the buffer representative at position 8(_i_-1) in _L_, placing \(R'_i\) at the front of _Li<sub>i</sub>_.

**iii.** Lastly, update \(s'_\#:=s_\#=2s'_\#\) to account for the resize.

After insertion, the global order of active representatives is preserved. The initial search step finds the last active representative \(\le x\) by _R._search(_x_), then _x_ is placed in the position directly after that position, ensuring the new active representative \(R'_z\) is constructed in its correct sorted position, obeying \(R'_{z-1}\le R'_z<R'_{z+1}\). The resize operation collects all active representatives in the rebuild buffer and then places each \(R'_i\) at position 8(_i_-1). Since the sequence 8(_i_-1) is monotone increasing with _i_, the active representatives appear in the same order as they were collected, maintaining the global sorted sequence \(R'_1\dots R'_{s_\#}\).

Let us now derive the standard cost of _R._insert(_x_) excluding the cost of dynamic rebalancing. The first step requires at most \(lgs'_\#+3\) comparisons by Lemma A.1. The second step requires exactly lg8=3 comparisons as 8 is a power of 2. The third step exchanges \(k-j+1\le 7\) active representatives, which requires _O_(lg_m_) comparisons and _O_(lg_m_) moves. Constructing the representative in step 4 requires _O_(lg_m_) moves. Verifying if _k\<_8 was violated in step 5 requires only _O_(1) arithmetic operations.

The resize in step 6 is triggered following \(s'_\#\) insertions into the structure since the last resize. The initial scanning phase makes _k_ comparisons and _k_ exchanges for a gap containing _k_ active representatives, thus in total it makes exactly _s<sub>#</sub>_ comparisons and representative exchanges. Then, each active representative is exchanged back into the library. Spread among \(s'_\#\) insertions, using \(s_\#=2s'_\#\), this is 2 comparisons and 4 representative exchanges per insertion, which are _O_(lg_m_) comparisons and _O_(lg_m_) moves. Following the resize, \(s'_\#\) has doubled, and the structure requires \(s'_\#\) subsequent insertions to trigger another resize, which has equal amortized cost by the same argument.

## A.3 Rebalancing

We proceed to consider the process of dynamic rebalancing. Recall that we have an imaginary segment tree over the gaps \(L_1\dots L_{s_\#}^{^\prime}\) with nodes \(n_1\dots n_{2s_\#^{^\prime}-1}\), where _n_<sub>1</sub> is the root node covering all gaps, and leaf nodes \(n_{s_\#}^{^\prime}\dots n_{2s_\#^{^\prime}-1}\) correspond with individual gaps. For a node _n<sub>k</sub>_ covering the range \(L_\ell\dots L_r\), _n_<sub>2_k_</sub> is its left child covering the left half of the range \(L_\ell\dots L_{\lfloor(l+r)/2\rfloor}\), and _n_<sub>2_k_+1</sub> is its right child covering the right half of the range \(L_{\lfloor(l+r)/2\rfloor+1}\dots L_r\). This implies the sibling of a node _n<sub>k</sub>_ is \(n_{k\oplus 1}\) and its parent is \(n_{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\) covering the union of the ranges of its children _n<sub>k</sub>_ and \(n_{k\oplus 1}\). As \(s'_\#\) is a power of 2, the general

formula for the range covered by a node _nk_ is \(L_\ell\dots L_r\) where \(l=\left(k-2^{\lfloor lgk\rfloor}\right)2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgk\rfloor}+1\) and \(r=l+2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgk\rfloor}-1\). For a node _nk_ covering the range \(L_\ell\dots L_r\), we define size(_nk_) as the number of active representatives in the range covered by the node, that is the number of active representatives in \(L_\ell\dots L_r\), and span(_nk_) as the length of the range covered by the node, which is given by _r-l_+1 or \(2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgk\rfloor}\) from the general formulas of _l_ and _r_. As a parent covers the union of the ranges of its children, size(_nk_)=size(_n_2_k_)+size(_n_2_k_+1) and span(_nk_)=span(_n_2_k_)+span(_n_2_k_+1). Additionally, since each gap contains at least 1 active representative by the gap invariant, \(size(n_k)\ge span(n_k)\). This structure is not explicitly stored by the algorithm, but we logically traverse the tree during dynamic rebalancing. The key realization is that density-based balancing, e.g. in [2] are inherently limited to logarithmic slack, incurring an \(O(lglogs'_\#)\) comparisons overhead per search. Instead, we lazily keep nodes weight balanced, like scapegoat trees in [3]. For our structure, the invariant for some internal node _nk_ is \(|size(n_{2k})-size(n_{2k+1})|\le max\left(1,size(n_k)/logs'_\#\right)\) (A.1) We let _n_leaf be some leaf node in the tree whose ancestors all satisfy (A.1), and _ni_ be the shallowest ancestor of _n_leaf such that \(size(n_i)2_k_)+size(_n_2_k_+1)=size(_nk_), we bound the size of the children of a node _nk_ that follows (A.1) when \(size(n_k)\ge lgs'_\#\) \(max\left(size(n_{2k}),size(n_{2k+1})\right)\le\left(1+1/logs'_\#\right)size(n_k)/2\) By the above relationship, the size of a node reduces by a factor of at least \(\left(1+1/logs'_\#\right)/2\) per level of the tree given the size of the parent exceeds \(logs'_\#\), which is true for all \(\lfloor lgi\rfloor\) ancestors of _ni_ as sizes of nodes moving up the tree are monotone increasing. Thus, we bound size(_ni_) \(size(n_i)\le\left((1+1/logs'_\#)/2\right)^{\lfloor lgi\rfloor} s_\#\)
\(\le(1+1/logs'_\#)^{\lfloor lgi\rfloor} s_\#/2^{\lfloor lgi\rfloor}\) The expression (1+1_/u)u_ approaches _e_ from below, and since \(i\le 2s'_\#-1\) by the definition of the node indexes and \(s'_\#\) is a power of 2, we can deduce \(\lfloor lgi\rfloor\le lgs_\#\); thus \(\left(1+1/logs'_\#\right)^{\lfloor lgi\rfloor}\le\left(1+1/logs'_\#\right)^{logs^\prime_\#}\le e\), giving \(size(n_i)\le es_\#/2^{\lfloor lgi\rfloor}\) (A.2) For nodes _nk_ following (A.1) where \(size(n_k)k_)=size(_n_2_k_)+size(_n_2_k_+1), this implies \(max\left(size(n_{2k}),size(n_{2k+1})\right)\le\left(size(n_k)+1\right)/2\) Repeating this linear recurrence from _ni_ for the remaining \(logs'_\#-\lfloor lgi\rfloor\) layers of the tree until we reach _n_leaf yields by induction \(size(n_\text{leaf})\le\left(size(n_i)+\left(2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgi\rfloor}-1\right)\right)/2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgi\rfloor}\)
\(\le size(n_i)/2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgi\rfloor}+1\) Applying the size bounds for _ni_ in (A.2), we obtain \(size(n_\text{leaf})\le\left(es_\#/2^{\lfloor lgi\rfloor}\right)/2^{logs^\prime_\#-\lfloor lgi\rfloor}+1\)
\(\le es_\#/2^{logs^\prime_\#}+1\)

Using \(s_\#\le 2s'_\#\) yields the final bound for size(_n_leaf)

\(size\left(n_\text{leaf}\right)\le 2e+1\) (A.3)

This bound is critical in proving the existence of a scapegoat node, shown shortly. We will first describe the procedure for dynamic rebalancing on a full gap _L<sub>i</sub>_:

Firstly, initialize the procedure. We use the variables: _j_ to denote the current node in the traversal is _n<sub>j</sub>_, _z_ to denote the size of the node _n<sub>j</sub>_, and variables \(z'_1\) and \(z'_2\) to denote the size of the child nodes of _n<sub>j</sub>_, where \(z'_1\) and \(z'_2\) can correspond to any child. We begin at the leaf node _n<sub>j</sub>_ that corresponds to the full gap _L<sub>i</sub>_, so \(j=i+s'_\#-1\) and _z_=8.

Secondly, traverse to the parent of the current node _n<sub>j</sub>_. Set \(z'_1:=z=size\left(n_j\right)\), and \(z'_2:=size\left(n_{j\oplus 1}\right)\). To find \(size\left(n_{j\oplus 1}\right)\), first set \(z'_2:=0\), then use the general formula to find the range \(L_\ell\dots L_r\) covered by \(n_{j\oplus 1}\), and iterate through all gaps in \(L_\ell\dots L_r\), where for each gap a linear scan from \(\ell_2\) counts the number of active representatives in the gap and adds it to \(z'_2\) (similar to during resizes, but without exchanging active representatives). This process requires \(size\left(n_{j\oplus 1}\right)=z'_2\) comparisons. Lastly, set \(j:=\lfloor j/2\rfloor\), moving the current node marker to the parent of the current node, then \(\{z'_1,z'_2\}=\{size\left(n_{2j}\right),size\left(n_{2j+1}\right)\}\), which are correctly the size of the two children of _n<sub>j</sub>_. As _n<sub>j</sub>_ covers the union of the ranges of its children, calculate \(z:=z'_1+z'_2\). This moves the current node to its parent node whilst maintaining the correctness of all variables.

Thirdly, verify if the current node _n<sub>j</sub>_ obeys the requirement

\(|size\left(n_{2j}\right)-size\left(n_{2j+1}\right)|>max\left(1,size\left(n_j\right)/lgs'_\#\right)\) (A.4)

Here we do not need to recompute the sizes of the nodes, as they are already computed and stored in _z_, \(z'_1\) and \(z'_2\). As size(_n_<sub>2_j_</sub>) and size(_n_<sub>2_j_+1</sub>) are interchangeable in (A.4), the lack of differentiation between the left and right children of _n<sub>j</sub>_ in \(z'_1\) and \(z'_2\) does not matter. If the requirements are met, _n<sub>j</sub>_ is the scapegoat node, and we rebuild the subtree rooted at the _n<sub>j</sub>_, distributing active representatives under _n<sub>j</sub>_ as evenly as possible, then terminate. Otherwise, return to step 2 and continue traversing upwards the tree.

Given that _L<sub>i</sub>_ is full, a scapegoat node that obeys these requirements must exist. Condition (A.4) is the negation of the invariant (A.1); a node that violates (A.1) satisfies (A.4). By (A.3), if all ancestors of _L<sub>i</sub>_ obey the invariant (A.1), the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_ is at most 2_e_+1. However, as _L<sub>i</sub>_ is full with 8_\>_2_e_+1 active representatives, we have a contradiction, and thus there must exist an ancestor that disobeys the invariant (A.1) and thus obeys (A.4).

## A.4 Rebuilding

The process for rebuilding the subtree rooted at the scapegoat node _n<sub>j</sub>_ covering the range \(L_\ell\dots L_r\) with _z_=size(_n<sub>j</sub>_) involves the following:

Firstly, by a linear scan of \(L_\ell\dots L_r\) identical to the scan in resizing, exchange all active representatives to a contiguous block _a_<sub>1</sub>_...a<sub>z</sub>_ at the front of _D_. Now the region \(L_\ell\dots L_r\) is composed entirely of buffer representatives.

Secondly, replace the active representatives into \(L_\ell\dots L_r\). For all gaps \(L_k\in L_\ell\dots L_r\) with the corresponding leaf node \(n_{k^\prime}\) (where \(k'=k+s'_\#-1\)) under _n<sub>j</sub>_, determine the active representatives \(a_{l^\prime}\dots a_{r^\prime}\) that should be in _L<sub>k</sub>_, and exchange them into the first \(r'-l'+1\) positions of _L<sub>k</sub>_. We cannot simply distribute them naively in the manner of [2] as the invariant (A.1) is based off weight instead of density which may remain violated even after a naive redistribution, thus we define \(a_{l^\prime}\dots a_{r^\prime}\) for all nodes in the subtree as follows:

The scapegoat node _n<sub>j</sub>_ trivially covers all active representatives _a_<sub>1</sub>_...a<sub>z</sub>_. For a node with current range \(a_{l^\prime}\dots a_{r^\prime}\), distribute the left half \(a_{l^\prime}\dots a_{\lfloor(l^\prime+r^\prime)/2\rfloor}\) to the left subtree

and the right half \(a_{\lfloor(l^\prime+r^\prime)/2\rfloor+1}\dots a_{r^\prime}\) to the right subtree. Rearranging, the left subtree receives \(\lfloor(r'-l')/2\rfloor+1\) active representatives and the right subtree \(\lceil(r'-l')/2\rceil\) active representatives. From the property \(0\le\lfloor(r'-l')/2\rfloor+1-\lceil(r'-l')/2\rceil\le 1\) for all positive integers \(l\le r\), for any node _nk_ in the rebuilt subtree \(0\le\mathrm{size}(n_{2k})-\mathrm{size}(n_{2k+1})\le 1\), spreading active representatives as evenly as possible, which guarantees the invariant (A.1) is upheld in the rebuilt subtree. To calculate the suitable range for all leaf nodes, we are unable to use the recursive method in \[3\] as it requires a recursion stack of _O_(lg_z_) words. Instead, we utilize a more complex method that requires a stack _K_ of only _O_(lg_z_) bits. Start by initializing \(l'=1\), \(r'=z\) and \(j'=j\) to denote the current node in the traversal is the scapegoat node _nj_ which should have all the collected active representatives _a_1_...az_ under it. _K_ is initially empty. We now describe three move primitives to move the current node \(n_{j^\prime}\) to the left child, right child, and parent node whilst updating the variables \(l'\) and \(r'\) correctly. We assume that \(j'\), \(l'\), \(r'\) and _K_ are stored in some scope such that they are accessible in the procedures. The procedure to move to the left child pushes \(\lfloor(r'-l')/2\rfloor+1-\lceil(r'-l')/2\rceil\) into _K_, then sets \(r':=\lfloor(l'+r')/2\rfloor\) and \(j':=2j'\). The procedure to move to the right child pushes \(\lfloor(r'-l')/2\rfloor+1-\lceil(r'-l')/2\rceil\) into _K_, then sets \(l':=\lfloor(l'+r')/2\rfloor+1\) and \(j':=2j'+1\). The procedure to move to the parent first reads the top of _K_ and stores it in a variable _d_, and pops the top of _K_. Then, if \(n'_j\) is a left child, which is the case when \(j'\) is even, set \(r':=r'+(r'-l'+1-d)\). Otherwise, \(n'_j\) is a right child and set \(l':=l'-(r'-l'+1+d)\). Lastly, set \(j':=\lfloor j'/2\rfloor\) regardless of which side \(n'_j\) is on. In the stack, we store the difference in sizes of the two child nodes for every ancestor of the current node \(n_{j^\prime}\) up to the scapegoat node _nj_. As \(0\le\lfloor(r'-l')/2\rfloor+1-\lceil(r'-l')/2\rceil\le 1\), this value is either 0 or 1, which can be represented using one bit. Since the height of the subtree rooted at _nj_ is \(\mathrm{lg}s'_\#-\lfloor\mathrm{lg}j\rfloor\le\mathrm{lg}m\), the entire stack fits in a single word of at least lg_m_ bits. Trivially, the procedures to move to the left child and right child give us the correct values \(l'\) and \(r'\) as they simply follow the definitions of \(l'\) and \(r'\). Using the stored difference in sizes and the property that the left child is always larger as \(\lfloor(r'-l')/2\rfloor+1\ge\lceil(r'-l')/2\rceil\), we can determine the range of active representatives distributed to the sibling node from the current node, and as the parent node contains the union of its children, this also allows us to determine the range of active representatives distributed to the parent node. We now show that moving to the parent correctly reverses moving to a child. We start by assuming the variables \(j'=j'_i\), \(l'=l'_i\) and \(r'=r'_i\) are in some arbitrary valid state. After we move to the left child, \(j'=2j'_i\), \(l'=l'_i\), \(r'=l'_i+\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor\), and we have \(\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor+1-\lceil(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rceil\) at the top of the stack. Then, if we move back to the parent, \(j'=\lfloor 2j'_i/2\rfloor=j'_i\), \(l'=l'_i\), and \(r'=l'_i+\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor\)
\(+(l'_i+\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor-l'_i+1-(\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor+1-\lceil(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rceil))\) Cancelling out complementary terms \(r'=l'_i+\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor+\lceil(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rceil\) Using \(\lfloor(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rfloor+\lceil(r'_i-l'_i)/2\rceil=r'_i-l'_i\) for all \(r'_i-l'_i\in\mathbb{Z}\), we obtain \(r'=r'_i\)

_K_ is also reverted to its initial state as the newly pushed value is popped out when we move back to the parent. By moving to the right child then back to the parent, the same equality \(j'=j'_i\), \(l'=l'_i\), \(r'=r'_i\) and unchanged _K_ holds. Thus, moving to the parent correctly reverses moving to a child.

By induction, starting from the root of the subtree _n<sub>j</sub>_ with the valid initialized ranges, any sequence of moving to the left child, right child, or parent yields a valid state with the correct block of active representatives \(a_{l^\prime}\dots a_{r^\prime}\) for the current node as long as the current node is a valid node in the subtree.

Using the above three move primitives, perform a standard in-order traversal of the subtree rooted at the scapegoat node. Upon reaching a leaf \(n_{j^\prime}\), exchange the active representatives \(a_{l^\prime}\dots a_{r^\prime}\) that should be in \(n_{j^\prime}\) into the first \(r'-l'+1\) positions of the leaf node \(n_{j^\prime}\)’s corresponding gap \(L_{j^{\prime\prime}-s_{\#}^\prime+1}\). We know that a node \(n_{j^\prime}\) is a leaf and has no more children if \(j'\ge s'_\#\) by the definition of the tree.

After dynamic rebalancing, the gap invariant is restored. Before the insertion, all gaps followed the gap invariant and contained less than 7 active representatives. The insertion altered the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_ to 8, triggering the rebalancing. Thus, viewing from the scapegoat node, the size of the child containing _L<sub>i</sub>_ is bounded by\(z'_1\le 7\left(span\left(n_{2j}\right)-1\right)+8=7span\left(n_{2j}\right)+1\), and the size of the other child is bounded by \(z'_2\le 7span\left(n_{2j}\right)\). By condition (A.4), we know the difference in sizes between the two children is at least 2. If \(z'_1>z'_2\), then \(z'_2\le z'_1-2=7span\left(n_{2j}\right)-1\), thus the size of the rebuilt subtree is given by \(z'_1+z'_2\le 2(7span\left(n_{2j}\right))=7span\left(n_j\right)\). In the latter case where \(z'_2>z'_1\), \(z'_1\le z'_2-2=7span\left(n_{2j}\right)-2\), and summing gives the bound \(z'_1+z'_2\le 2(7span\left(n_{2j}\right))-2\le 7span\left(n_j\right)\). Thus, this inequality connecting _z_=size(_n<sub>j</sub>_) and span(_n<sub>j</sub>_) holds in either case.

Because size (_n_<sub>2_k_</sub>)-size (\(n_{2k+1}\)) \(\le 1\) for all nodes in the rebuilt subtree, by induction it can be shown that any two nodes _n_<sub>_k_<sub>1</sub></sub> and _n_<sub>_k_<sub>2</sub></sub> on the same level in the rebuilt subtree obeys \(\left|size\left(n_{k_1}\right)-size\left(n_{k_2}\right)\right|\le 1\). Using this property, the size of a leaf node _n_<sub>leaf</sub> in the rebuilt subtree satisfies

\(size\left(n_\text{leaf}\right)\le\left[\text{size}\left(n_j\right)/span\left(n_j\right)\right]\)

Shown above size \(\left(n_j\right)\le 7span\left(n_j\right)\), so

\(size\left(n_\text{leaf}\right)\le 7\)

Likewise, the size of each leaf node is at least \(\left|size\left(n_j\right)/span\left(n_j\right)\right|\ge 1\) by size \(\left(n_j\right)\ge span\left(n_j\right)\). Thus, the gap invariant 0_\<k\<_8 is restored.

We also show that the rebuild does not change the order of active representatives. The linear scan collects active representatives from the subtree into the rebuild buffer in the same order as they appear in the library. At every step of the traversal downwards to the leaves, we distribute the left half of the active representatives to the left child, and the right half to the right child. By induction, for any two collected active representatives _a<sub>x</sub>_ and _a<sub>y</sub>_ where _x\<y_, _a<sub>x</sub>_ will be placed before _a<sub>y</sub>_ in the library, maintaining local order within the rebuilt subtree. Furthermore, as elements are only rearranged within the rebuilt subtree, global order is also maintained.

Now, let us evaluate the total cost of an instance of dynamic rebalancing.

At any step of the traversal, we set \(z'_1=z\), count \(z'_2=size\left(n_{j\oplus 1}\right)\) using \(z'_2\) comparisons, then set \(z=z'_1+z'_2\), increasing _z_ by \(z'_2\). Thus, it requires 1 comparison to count every additional active representative. Initially, the count starts at 8, thus we counted _z_-8 additional active representatives by this method, which requires _z_-8 comparisons in total. Arithmetic operations during traversal are negligible at _O_(1) per level traversed.

Then, the rebuild process first uses _z_ comparisons and _z_ representative exchanges to move all active representatives to _D_. After which, they are replaced back into the library. This process exchanges all _z_ representatives back into the library in their calculated positions using one exchange. By the standard analysis of traversing a binary tree in in-order, the move procedures are called _O(z_) times, and each use requires _O_(1) arithmetic operations, totaling _O(z_) arithmetic operations. Summing up, dynamic rebalancing makes _O(z_lg_m_) comparisons, _O(z_lg_m_) moves, and _O(z_lg_m_) arithmetic operations.

As the traversal phase does not make any moves, it cannot change the order of active representatives, and as rebuilds do not change the order of active representatives, active representatives remain in sorted order after dynamic rebalancing.

## A.5 Amortized Analysis

Although individual instances of dynamic rebalancing can cost up to _O(s_#lg_m_) when the root is rebuilt, as large rebuilds are rare, the amortized cost of dynamic rebalancing is small. While the main text provides an intuitive bound using a simplified accounting method, here we formalize this proof via a potential argument.

For an internal node _n<sub>k</sub>_, let the imbalance of _n<sub>k</sub>_ be defined as

\(\psi\left(n_k\right)=max\left(0,\left|size\left(n_{2k}\right)-size\left(n_{2k+1}\right)\right|-1\right)\) (A.5)

This allows us to define our non-negative potential function for some scaling constant _c_:

\(\Phi=\sum_{i=1}^{s_\#^{-1}}c\cdot\psi(n_i)lg^2s'_\#.\) (A.6)

When a new active representative is inserted into a gap _L<sub>i</sub>_, the size of that leaf node and all its ancestors increases by 1. For each of the \(lgs'_\#\) ancestors of _L<sub>i</sub>_, exactly one child’s size increases by 1, which may cause its imbalance to increase by 1. This, in turn may increase potential by \(clgs'_\#lg^2s'_\#=clg^3s'_\#\). Recall previously that the baseline actual cost of insertion, i.e. excluding dynamic rebalancing is _O_(lg_m_). By definition, the amortized cost is given by the actual cost of the operation plus the change in the potential function (\(\Delta\Phi\)). Thus, the aggregate cost of insertion prior to the rebuild is given by:

\(O(lgm)+clg^3s'_\#=O(lg^3m).\)

When a rebuild occurs, the found scapegoat node _n<sub>j</sub>_ has \(\psi\left(n_j\right)=\Omega(z/logs'_\#)\) by condition (A.4). After rebuilding the subtree rooted in _n<sub>j</sub>_, all internal nodes _n<sub>k</sub>_ within the rebuilt topology obey \(\left|size\left(n_{2k}\right)-size\left(n_{2k+1}\right)\right|\le 1\), strictly reducing the internal potential of the subtree to 0. Because the total size of the subtree rooted at _n<sub>j</sub>_ is strictly conserved during the local structural change, the sizes and imbalances of all ancestors of _n<sub>j</sub>_ remain completely unaffected. Since all node potentials are non-negative, the total drop in the global potential \(\Phi\) is bounded below by the drop at _n<sub>j</sub>_ itself, which is \(c\cdot\psi\left(n_j\right)lg^2s'_\#=c\cdot\Omega(zlogs'_\#)=c\cdot\Omega(zlgm)\). By selecting the scaling constant _c_ to be sufficiently large, the net decrease in \(\Phi\) absorbs the _O(z_lg_m_) actual cost of the rebuild. Thus, the rebuild step contributes nothing (or a negative amount) to the aggregate amortized cost. This means the total amortized cost of insertion, including any dynamic rebalancing it may trigger, is strictly bounded by the baseline cost.

Resizes cannot increase potential as they re-initialize all gaps uniformly with 1 active representative per gap which represents a perfectly balanced state where potential is 0. Thus, the aggregate cost stands.

## D In-Place Conversion

We now present the process for converting the algorithm that uses additional buffers in Section 2 to the full in-place algorithm in Section 3.

As stated in Section 3, the buffer memory is made up of buffer elements, which are all greater or equal to a pivot _p_, whilst all active elements are less than _p_, allowing active and buffer elements to be differentiated via 1 comparison against _p_.

The bit vector _V_ is also formed by two blocks _L_ and _R_, where the pair of elements (_l<sub>i</sub>,r<sub>i</sub>_) are used to represent the _i_th bit. Initially, every element in _L_ needs to be strictly less than every element in _R_ (so no pair can be equal).

We now show how these regions are created, beginning with the bit vector. Using heapselect, select the smallest and largest _v=n/_lg<sup>2</sup>_n_ elements and place them in contiguous blocks at the front and back of A, changing the configuration of A to \(LA'R\). We use a single comparison to verify if the last element in _L_ is strictly less than the first element of _R_. If so, the block \(A'\) contains only equal values, then the entire input array is already sorted, and the algorithm terminates. Conversely, if the blocks _L_ and _R_ pass the test above, they can be used to simulate a bit vector of _n/_lg<sup>2</sup>_n_ bits. As \(m\le n\), the bit vector is sufficiently large for all instances of sorting. This step requires _O(n+v_lg_n_)=_O(n_) comparisons and moves.

Now, we repeatedly create active and buffer regions in a partition-based loop. At any iteration, the configuration of \(A'\) is _AS<sub>U</sub>_, where _AS<sub>S</sub>_ contains elements in their correct sorted position and _A<sub>U</sub>_ unsorted elements. Particularly, if _A<sub>U</sub>_ were sorted using some algorithm, the entire block \(A'\) would be sorted, and _A_ would also be sorted as a whole. Initially, _AS<sub>S</sub>_ is empty and _A<sub>U</sub>_ contains the entire block \(A'\). Every iteration shrinks the size of _A<sub>U</sub>_ by a factor of at least 1/4, until eventually \(|A_U|\le 2^{19}=524288\), then the entire _A<sub>U</sub>_ is sorted as a base case. The process for the _i_th iteration, where _n<sub>i</sub>_=|_A<sub>U</sub>|_, is as follows:

**1.** By the in-place selection algorithm of [5], find the element _p_ in _A<sub>U</sub>_ with rank \(\lceil n_i/4\rceil\).

**2.** Partition _A<sub>U</sub>_ by pivot _p_, such that the configuration of _A<sub>U</sub>_ becomes \(A_< pB_\ge\), where _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></o><sub></sub> contains elements _\<p_, and \(B_\ge\) contains elements \(\ge p\). We denote |_A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>|=n<sub>i</o>,<o></o>_ and \(|B_\ge|=n_{i,\ge}\). As _p_ has rank \(\lceil n_i/4\rceil\), \(n_{i,<}\le\lceil n_i/4\rceil-1\le n_i/4\), then \(n_{i,\ge}\ge n_i-\lceil n_i/4\rceil\ge(3/4)n_i-1\).

**3.** Sort the block _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></o><sub></sub>_ by the algorithm from Section 2, using the blocks _L_ and _R_ to simulate the bit vector _V_ , and \(B_\ge\) as the buffer memory. We can differentiate active elements originating from _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>_ with buffer elements originating from \(B_\ge\) by a single comparison against _p_. As \(n_{i,\ge}\ge 3n_i/4-1=3n_{i,<}-1\), \(B_\ge\) is indeed adequately large to function as the buffer memory to sort _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub><sub></sub>_. This leaves _A<sub>U</sub>_ in the form _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>,<o>S</o>_\(B'_\ge\), where _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></o>,<o>S</o>_ is the sorted sequence _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>_ and \(B'_\ge\) is some permutation of \(B_\ge\).

**4.** Partitioning \(B'_\ge\) by pivot _p_, we isolate all elements =_p_ in \(B'_\ge\). The resulting structure of _A<sub>U</sub>_ is _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>,<o>S</o>_\(pPB_\ge\), where _P_ contains _n<sub>i,</sub>_= elements which are =_p_ and _B<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub><sub></sub>_ contains _n<sub>i,</sub>_ elements that are _\>p_.

**5.** Notice that the elements _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>,<o>S</o><sub></sub>_\(pP\) are already in their correct sorted order, thus we update _AS<sub>S</sub>_ to include _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub>,<o>S</o>_\(pP\), and shrink _A<sub>U</sub>_ to only include _B<sub>><o>A</o><sub></sub><sub></sub>_, then start a new iteration with _n<sub>i</sub>_+1=|_B<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub></sub>|_. If \(n_{i+1}\le 2^{19}\), we sort the entire _A<sub>U</sub>_ by the method in Section 2.7 without using a buffer, then terminate. As _p_ has rank \(\lceil n_i/4\rceil\), \(|B_\ge|\le n_i-\lceil n_i/4\rceil\le(3/4)n_i\).

We now calculate the cost of a single iteration. The in-place selection of _p_ requires _O(n_) comparisons and \(\varepsilon n\) moves by [5]. Then, partitioning _A<sub>U</sub>_ requires _n<sub>i</sub>_ comparisons and 2_n<sub>i,</sub>_+1 moves. Let \(C'(m)\) and \(M'(m)\) denote the number of comparisons and moves respectively to sort a block of size _m_ with additional memory. Then, sorting _A<sub><o>A</o><sub></sub><sub></sub>_ using

the buffer memories in step 3 requires \(C'(n_{i,<})\) comparisons and \(M'(n_{i,<})\) moves. Lastly, partitioning \(B_\ge\) to remove equal elements requires \(n_{i,\ge}\) comparisons and 2_n__i,_=+1 moves. By straightforward induction, we bound \(n_i\le(3/4)^in\). With _I_ as the number of iterations, we have \(\sum_{i=1}^In_i\le n\sum_{i=1}^I\left(3/4\right)^i\le n/(1-3/4)=4n\) (D.1) As every iteration expands _AS_ by _n__i,\<<_+_n__i,_=+1 until its size reaches \(|\mathcal{A}'|\) and the algorithm terminates, then \(\sum_{i=1}^In_{i,<}\le\left(\sum_{i=1}^In_{i,<}+n_{i,=}+1\right)=|\mathcal{A}'|\le n\) (D.2) Summing over all iterations, the number of comparisons _C(n_) to sort the input array _A_ is \(C(n)=O(n)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^IO(n_i)+n_i+C'\left(n_{i,<}\right)+n_{i,\ge}\right)\)
\(=O(n)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^IC'\left(n_{i,<}\right)+O(n_i)\right)\) Applying (D.1), we obtain \(C(n)=O(n)+\sum_{i=1}^IC'(n_{i,<})\) Let _F(m_) denote all terms in \(C'(m)\) that grow super-linearly. From Theorems 2.6 and 2.7, _F(m_)=_m_lg_m_ or _F(m_)=_m_lg_m+m_lg(_t_)_m_. Separating \(C'(n_{i,<})\) gives: \(C(n)=O(n)+\sum_{i=1}^I\left(F(n_{i,<})+O(n_{i,<})\right)\) For both variations of _F(m_), the expression _F(m)/m_ is non-decreasing when _F(m_) is well defined. Therefore, _F(m_) is superadditive. Using (D.2) and the superadditivity of _F(m_): \(C(n)\le F(n)+O(n)=C'(n)+O(n).\) By a parallel derivation for the moves _M(n_) (note that _F(m_)=0 as \(M'(m)\) grows linearly with _m_) \(M(n)=O(n)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^I\varepsilon n_i+2n_{i,<}+1+M'\left(n_{i,<}\right)+2n_{i,=}+1\right)\)
\(\le M'(n)+O(n).\) (Where \(\varepsilon>0\) denotes an arbitrarily small, but fixed, real constant.) \(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma D.1.** _The input array_ A _can be sorted in-place using no more than_ \(C'(n)+O(n)\) _comparisons and_ \(M'(n)+O(n)\) _moves given an algorithm that sorts a sequence of m elements with additional memory using_ \(C'(m)\) _comparisons and_ \(M'(m)\) _moves._
